title: Hand and day
goal: Complete all five noun groups with the fourth and fifth declensions, then express time in two different ways.
bekal: recognize *manus* and *dies* as groups of their own, not spelling mistakes
tell "when" from "how long" by the form of the noun
name seasons, months, and dates the Roman way

dialogs.title: Colloquium — In villa, quinque dies
dialogs.intro: Day two at the farmhouse. The weather is lovely, and everyone has an opinion about the seasons.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: How many days will we stay here?

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: Quinque dies. Post quinque dies domum redibimus.
lines.id: Five days. After five days we'll go home.

notes: **Manus ends in -us, but it isn't second declension.** Compare *hortus, horti* (group two) with *manus, manus* (group four). As always, the "of" form tells them apart. If you treat *manus* as group two, you'll write *mani*, which doesn't exist in Latin.

**Vere, aestate, hieme, autumno — seasons use the with/in form.** To say when something happens, Latin uses the with/in form with no preposition at all: *hieme* ("in winter"), *nocte* ("at night"), *hora prima* ("at the first hour").

**Duas horas natabas — "how long" uses the object form.** Note the difference from the note above. *Hora prima* means "at the first hour"; *duas horas* means "for two hours". One question asks for a point in time, the other for its length, and Latin uses two different forms for them.

**Res, spes, fides — three big words from the fifth group.** This group has the fewest members but contains some of the most quoted words: *res* (thing, matter), *spes* (hope), *fides* (trust, loyalty), and *dies* (day). From *res* comes *res publica* — "the public matter" — which became the word *republic*.

blocks.text: These last two groups have few words, but the words are common. Both are easy to spot by their "of" form: *-us* for group four, *-ei* for group five.

*Manus* uses the same form for four different jobs — subject singular, "of" singular, subject plural, and object plural. That sounds scary, but in real sentences it's never a problem: the verbs and adjectives around it always tell you which one it is.

*Domus* ("house") is a mix: some of its forms are group four, some group two. For now just learn its three frozen forms you've used since Unit 5: *domi* (at home), *domum* (home, homeward), *domo* (from home).
Two questions about time are answered with two different forms, and neither uses a preposition.

Roman dates were counted backward from three fixed points each month: the *Kalendae* (the 1st), the *Nonae* (the 5th or 7th), and the *Idus* (the 13th or 15th). *Idus Martiae* — the Ides of March, the day Caesar was killed — is March 15. This countdown system is complicated and isn't practiced in this book, but the three names are worth knowing because they come up often.
*Res* is the most flexible word in Latin. It means "thing", but what it refers to depends on the words around it, and many of these phrases are still alive today.

blocks.text: Look at *res novae*. To a Roman, "new things" was not praise but an accusation: people who wanted *res novae* wanted to turn the order upside down. The word *revolution* still carries that tension today.

blocks.title: Four time phrases worth memorizing
items: *hoc tempore* — at this time. *illo tempore* — at that time.
*multos annos* — for many years. *paucos dies* — for a few days.
*in dies* — day by day, more and more.
*ad tempus* — for the time being. *ante tempus* — before its time.
